utterances.text: Paragraph 117, same day, meeting with Lukic to establish a rapport and to discuss the level of MUP forces in Malisevo, you proposing a reduction. His reaction?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Malisevo was quite a long way to the west and had got a very substantial police presence there, which was more of a garrison than a police station, and the presence of those police in those numbers was acting as a deterrent to any of the Albanians going back to the village. And so I was trying to persuade him to reduce the level of presence and the way it operated, which was very aggressively, in that area. And Lukic said no, he would not reduce the presence, and I got the firm impression that this was a decision he could make, that he was deciding he would not, but he did not indicate he would have to clear this sort of proposal with anyone more senior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 119 is a meeting -- was it the first meeting you had with Walker and the KLA, I think at night?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the afternoon of the 25th of December, when the situation again started to be tense and started to flare up. Walker and I went up to Podujevo, and Walker decided that he would personally go and see the local KLA commander, which was a departure from what had been the practice up until that moment. So we went into the village where the KLA were and a meeting took place, and this was really the point at which we started to leave liaison officers with the KLA in order to communicate things to them rapidly, using our communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 120. You refer to the fact that on the 29th of December, the situation report - which I don't think we've actually got produced, but you've actually seen it - recorded the situation was quiet, when there were five murders, and you say that should compare with what happened a month earlier, when one killing would have excited interest.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is simply a comment, looking back on it, that what was regarded as almost commonplace by the end of December was very seriously more violent than the situation only about three weeks earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 121. Sainovic was seen in Pristina, but not to make contact with you or the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. We got the -- no. I was told by Loncar that he often had to go and see Sainovic, and then within an hour I might see him again, he having seen Sainovic, and so it was clear that Sainovic was not in Belgrade but in Pristina. But Sainovic did not take the opportunity to ever go and see Walker or deal directly with the Kosovo Verification Mission. Loncar continued to be the intermediary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then relations finally broke down --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- Sainovic and Walker after Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next Exhibit, please, tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, we're going to have to deal with exhibits, which will, of course, remain with the Chamber, to consider as swiftly as we can, because they can consume a lot of time. This is a document that I think you hadn't seen until --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That is correct. This is the Serbian version of one of the meetings between General Loncar and myself in December, and I only saw it before Easter, but I do recall the meeting, and I think the significant aspect of this meeting is that it is faithfully recorded in that I was at this stage using the words "disproportionate use of force" when we were discussing the actions of the Yugoslav forces in the area west of Podujevo. I did this because there had already been instances of the FRY forces using heavy weapons against villages which were known to contain civilians, and there had been instances both of heavy mortars being used and of tank main armament, in other words, the sort of -- the 100-millimetre shell that a tank will fire through its main gun rather than simply using its machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see your use of "disproportionate" five lines up from the bottom of the first page, but otherwise you think it's a faithful account --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- a faithful account of the meeting? Thank you. Was any permission given to you - I think this may be dealt with as well -- to visit the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- captives?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: There were regular requests to have contact with the KLA who had been captured in the border ambush, the nine, asking if we could go and see them and check on their condition, and this was constantly denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 125. As things were deteriorating - and we're now in late December - in Podujevo, an elderly Serbian man had been shot, I think.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This led to a discussion in Walker's office between Loncar and Kotur at how the recovery of the body should take place. We were concerned about it because we knew that this was a largely Kosovar Albanian village, and therefore to send in a large force of police and army would aggravate the situation. As I recall it, the Serb had been -- had been firing at Albanians himself and had then been shot in something that was quite local. And there was a plan that was described by Loncar, saying that about 15 vehicles of various sorts were going to be sent in in order to recover the body, and we were arguing that a smaller delegation would be less provocative and would allow the incident to be defused more rapidly. We thought we had reached an agreement that the recovery of this body, which was clearly important, would be carried out in a low-key way, and we were discussing things like what the exact number of vehicles was, which vehicles were going to lead, was it going to be ours or -- which we felt it should be. And as we were going through this discussion, the telephone rang, and we were told that in fact this operation had gone ahead as originally conceived, that a large number of police with armoured vehicles had entered the village and a firefight had erupted in the village. So this caused Walker to lose patience with General Loncar and basically said what was the point of us trying to work out this sort of detail, to try and keep a lid on the violence when, in fact, operations were going on behind our back, in effect. The meeting became ill-tempered. Kotur, in the course as we were all leaving, turned to me and said, "Police; you just can't trust them." And was saying, "Well, the left hand doesn't know what the right hand is doing." Loncar was adamant that the police were using their own chain of command, but it was my impression that this was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because? And that would have required independent actions by the police --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- commander in --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The point was that everything in this area was done with the -- in the presence of the VJ, who were manning the heavy weapons on the high ground. And therefore, to carry out an operation without the knowledge and cooperation of the people who were there to give you support from heavy weapons if you needed it would have been most unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had five or six days of home leave between the 30th of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. December and the 31st -- and the 6th of January of 1999. Then we come, I think, to the next exhibit, please. Tab 8. OTP reference 1567. This is an OSCE daily report, summarising the activities of a day when you were still on leave, but, nevertheless, you can help us with it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In particular, it's the Racak area that I think on page --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This report is the first indication in an OSCE report that the police were stepping up levels of activity in the Racak area, and it specifically mentions an observation point in the mental hospital which had excellent fields of view to the west towards Racak and the road that runs west from Stimlje through Suva Reka through the Dulje Heights, which was an area where clashes between the UCK and the security force -- the Yugoslav security forces took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't yet had any evidence, I think, about Racak. Yours will be the first.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going to -- when we see the plans, either through you or through another witness, we'll find that the mental hospital is a significant feature on the road there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. It is on the south-west outskirts of Stimlje. And so as you look west from the mental hospital, you can see over the open fields to the west, which -- and to the south, which takes you to Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next exhibit, please, tab 9. Another OSCE report three days later. 6th of January, covering the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This is the first report in which we saw a report of a policeman wearing what's described as a grey jumpsuit in the Decani area, and it is also the first -- so this is the first sighting of the special police unit which we believe carried out the action at Rogovo in late January. It also, on Racak, describes the food situation there as being critical, and that was certainly reflected by the -- my discussions with the UNHCR who were moving food into that area at various times over this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You just immediately look at page 2 of the document. Just -- that's the passage in the Pec district.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Alternative MUP clothing, one policeman seen wearing a grey jumpsuit is set out.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Paragraph 137. You started to receive, on the 8th of January, reports about roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This was the first action that involved Serbian civilians in the area south of Pristina, to the south and to the south-west, and these roadblocks of local vigilantes, many of them wearing masks over their faces, effectively closed off all communication between Pristina and any area to the south. So it actually cut all communications between Pristina and Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The explanation paragraph, 138, by the "authorities," being what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was described to me as being a spontaneous civilian demonstration which was protesting against government inactivity against the KLA. The -- I went out to see what exactly was happening on the ground and found myself watching Serb paramilitaries driving around in Golfs with their black ski masks on, carrying Kalashnikovs and would move to an area and then harangue the local civilians to get them, to persuade them to erect a roadblock. And this organising of roadblocks was seen by me at a couple of locations. The interesting thing was this was one of the few moments when civic disorder took place and the police were not present to deal with it, because quite -- there were normally enough police present to be able to deal with any civil disorder, but the police were noticeably absent at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 140. I don't think I need to trouble with that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 141. On the 8th of January, during a meeting with Loncar --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This was a meeting, one of the regular meetings I was having with Loncar, and in the course of it there was a telephone call which Loncar took and then -- and he said, "There has been an incident." And shortly after that, the police colonel, Colonel Mijatovic, entered the room and said that three policemen had been killed in the area of Dulje, which is in the high ground between Suva Reka and Stimlje, quite close to Stimlje, and that there had been a daytime ambush of a police patrol and that these three policemen had been killed in that ambush. This is significant because it was the biggest daytime attack by the Kosovo Liberation Army that we had witnessed upon the police and was clearly a serious escalation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let's move to the next exhibit, which is tab 10, OTP reference 1580, a document again you hadn't seen until recently.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This is the description of that meeting. And the meeting -- as you say, I had not seen this document before the period just before Easter of this year, but the purpose of the meeting was a follow-up to the roadblocks established by the paramilitaries, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just for good order, we make sure we don't go too fast, if the first page of it is on the overhead projector, we can see just a little bit further down there's your name and the way you're being recorded as expressing concern over the roadblocks and so on. Can you carry on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. The other point that I brought up was that we were getting evidence from our people on the ground that the Yugoslav army was looting property when it was searching areas, and I was making the point that this was not acceptable and would -- would bring their forces into disrepute and that this should be investigated and proper instructions issued to make sure that didn't happen. We were then talking about the number of VJ that were out of barracks, and my point there was that the original agreement that we were still, as far as we were concerned, adhering to was that three company positions were allowed but that the area south of Podujevo had now been established as a fourth location at which there was a strong VJ presence out of barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we go to page 5 of the exhibit, please. This meeting, I think, was interrupted, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That's correct. And this is the moment which --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, six. That's during the discussion. "During the discussion, Loncar was informed over the telephone that three policemen had been killed, two seriously injured, between Suva Reka and Stimlje. Loncar said with concern that we will use tanks and the army and not the police in our search for the killers in order to find them." It is certainly of note that that was what was stated. I did not specifically react to that because he was clearly distressed, and I did not take that as -- as a declaration of intent but, rather, that -- because it was a very serious incident, that they would take all steps necessary to track down the killers. And that was, in my mind, a -- a natural reaction in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we pass from this exhibit, just a little bit further down the page, I think, or thereabouts, you've had the experience, interesting or otherwise, of seeing, after the event, what other people were writing about you. You see their observation here that you were using the KVM in respect of promotion, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think you need protest too much about any of that as a Major General at the time but to just tell us what was his position.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, I think my -- my reaction to this was to be somewhat upset, having actually been in the Balkans for 22 of the 28 months preceding, since October 1996. I felt that I was there because the OSCE knew me and trusted me as being someone who was quite good at dealing with civilian organisations. I did feel that at the time I was sensitive to the -- the local situation, and I felt that we should be taking every measure possible to prevent the situation from spiralling upward and out of control, and this was really why I had -- I had been prepared to go and join this mission at six hours' notice, at a time when I thought I was about to go to a more normal teaching job. So it wasn't how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we needn't cover that. Paragraph 143, and the next exhibit, which is tab 11, OTP reference 2794. It is a press release that was put out, condemning that ceasefire breach.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This is important, because it was often alleged that we did not condemn the actions of the insurgents when they -- when they carried out actions but we only condemned the actions of the Yugoslav forces. And I think this is quite clear as stating it strongly condemns an unacceptable breach of the ceasefire in that the three police were killed. Further down: "The KVM considers that such terrorist attacks and breaches of ceasefire undermine attempts to reach a political solution of the conflict." So I think this was a very clear statement which was in no way sympathetic to the insurgents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Deal very briefly, in summary, negotiations, paragraph 144, over the VJ prisoners over the next five days.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then -- again, I don't think we need the detail of that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think the point here was that we invested a lot of effort into getting the -- securing the release of the eight VJ soldiers who were held prisoner by the Kosovo Liberation Army. There were many moments when we thought that the army and police would storm the position. We literally interposed ourselves between the two sides and attempted to talk the situation down. I personally slept on the floor of my office for three nights in order to be there if telephone messages were received, and eventually, as a result of extensive negotiations, the release of those eight soldiers was -- was secured, and we were able to bring them off the mountain and hand them over to their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next exhibit, please, tab 12, OTP reference 1582. Just to deal with the reporting structure, there were daily reports and there were also summarising periodic reports. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This periodic report is really dealing with a specific highlight describing firstly the meeting between Principal Deputy Head of Mission Keller, who was the French Deputy Head of Mission, to Walker, and Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic in which the strong day-to-day control that Sainovic appears to have exercised comes out, I think. We also, in this, describe the state of VJ forces out of the barracks, which we equated to the equivalent of about six companies, remembering still that the agreement called for only three.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we just find that in the document, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. If we go to page -- paragraph 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: -- second subparagraph, paragraph 4, states that KVM patrols report a battalion-sized VJ deployment in the area of Podujevo. It is that battalion-sized deployment by which we would mean about three companies, to be in addition to the three that were authorised. So those three plus the original three make the six that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then the last page of the document, in case people want to track this at any time, records the KVM force at 682 by this time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 149 deals with the exchange of the eight VJ for nine KLA.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. And at that point, the tension certainly did reduce and there were the beginnings of indications that the VJ and MUP forces were starting to return to barracks, particularly in the area around Mitrovica. So at the time, this was seen as an encouraging sign and was certainly the result of a lot of hard negotiation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: However, you received a report which was perhaps less encouraging or more discouraging.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This was a telephone call from the American military attache in Belgrade, who reported that he had observed an armoured column on its way on the main Belgrade-to-Nis road, which by this stage had passed Nis and by this stage was within 20 miles of Kosovo. Our concern - because this was when we were in the middle of attempting to get the eight VJ soldiers off the top of a hill where the KLA were holding them - was that this was going to seriously complicate the situation if extra forces started to appear from outside. And I brought this up with General Loncar and was assured by him that they were not going to cross into Kosovo. And I said, "Fine, but you're really not sending the right message in deploying these sort of units so close to Kosovo when we are trying to bring this situation to a negotiated solution."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next exhibit - but we won't be looking, I think, at any part of it particularly - is an eight-page document, tab 13, OTP reference 2795. This is a report on the ambush and subsequent hostage-taking incident of the 8th and 9th of January. It gives a chronology of the capture and negotiation surrounding the release of the eight VJ soldiers, which we've taken this morning in summary because we want to deal with it in that way. This report was prepared by whom, General?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was prepared by one of the liaison officers who worked directly for me, and was prepared on my instruction because it was important that we just reminded ourselves of the chronology of this thing, because by this stage, we were really all quite tired and there was a danger that we were going to forget where we were, quite frankly. And so -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we need to look for detail of that exchange, we can probably find it in this document.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I remember using this at the time as my aide-memoire, and it was a document that was constantly updated, and this is the final version of it, but it certainly reflects how we felt at the time on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit tab 14, a daily report this time for the 11th of January but covering the 10th.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the passage we particularly want to look at relates to the VJ MUP full-scale combat potential. Can you just take us to that, if you can find it. Certainly it's covered on the assessment in the first --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I think it must be the assessment. Let me just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see on the first page: "Tensions remain high in the Stimlje area as a result of the two ambushes."

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. I've got it now. "Tensions remain high in the Stimlje area as a result of the two ambushes against MUP patrols within the last three days. Strong VJ and MUP forces remain in the area. A report of increased VJ logistical support moving into the area indicates that the VJ are 'repaired' --" by which I think it means "prepared" "-- to remain deployed for an extended period." And then Pec is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. That was --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The report also describes places where the KVM, in trying to get to investigate events, was having its freedom of movement beginning to be curtailed. And again, this is one of the early indications of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next exhibit, please. Tab 15, OTP reference 1584. A short addendum to the daily update.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This was an irregular report put out if there was a feeling that we needed to just get everybody aware of an increase or a change in the security situation, and so given that the VJ and the MUP were increasing their activity, this was put out to make sure everybody was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 16 deals with - OTP reference 1586 - deals with a meeting between yourself and General Loncar on the 11th of January.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Again, this is one I did not see until March of this year, but this was our last meeting in the five-day process of getting the eight soldiers off the top of the hill. And again, reference is made to everything being done at the behest of Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's on page 2, I think you'll find, and also 3. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, that is. We wanted to resolve the problem in a peaceful manner, in a manner agreed upon in yesterday's discussions between Vice Premier Sainovic and Keller and Hill, Hill being the American ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit tab 17, a report for the period covered by the 12th of January in our report from the OSCE again.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: And the point of note here is the KVM patrols from Pristina and Prizren confirm the increase of VJ activity in the Stimlje area. Movement of armoured vehicles, including tanks, have been observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 2, paragraph 4. So this is all in the Racak build-up, really, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you recall the state of concern or anxiety by OSCE at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. At this point, we were covering in some strength the area in the west, the three counties in Kosovo in the west, which were the areas where the fighting had been worst in the summer. We were not in great strength in the rest of Kosovo, in the east of Kosovo, because that was not an area where there had been big problems or a very large KLA presence. And so as we built up, we were putting down a field presence in the areas in order of priority. The area of Racak and Stimlje were not actually yet in an area where we had got very substantial coverage. As events deteriorated in that area, we put more people into the area, but it was happening in an area where our coverage was less good than it was in the west, in the Pec and Decani area, where the problems had been worst, and therefore, where we had gone to in greater strength most early.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exhibit is tab 18. This is another meeting, this time -- sorry. It's a meeting evidenced by the Serbs and not seen by you until very recently.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That is correct, and this again simply describes the situation as it was seen by another member of the Kosovo Verification Mission on the 11th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because although you were present at this meeting --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, you weren't present. This is Nikolaev.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I think it's useful really only in describing the situation as seen by others than myself on the 11th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Consistent or inconsistent with your own --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It's entirely consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's available for that purpose of checking, then, if required. Paragraph 160. The nine KLA prisoners were, I think, exposed to a visit by your deputy or one of your liaison officers, Ciaglinski?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And although we may hear from Mr. Ciaglinski himself, reported back to you was what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This referred to the nine KLA who had been taken prisoner in December in the border ambush, and in the course of this, in January, we were told that they could now be seen and identified and spoken to, provided it was done by someone who was entirely discreet, and that was why I sent Richard Ciaglinski, who is someone with whom I dealt with daily. Ciaglinski travelled immediately to Nis and saw the nine prisoners. They stated - and this confirmed what we had learned up until then - that they had been part of a resupply column of the KLA that was moving supplies from Albania into Kosovo. They stated that they had been recruited quite reluctantly and had gone to Albania and been given no more than two days' training before they were sent on the supply mission. They had been armed but had not had very much training on how to use their weapons, so that when they walked into the ambush in the middle of the night, they simply dropped their weapons and ran. The conversations that Ciaglinski had with them, which were consistent, said that about 90 had run away and that about 40 had been killed or captured, and Ciaglinski had revisited the prisoners at a later date, and of course these were eventually handed over in a response to the handing over of the eight VJ soldiers subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed after Racak, as it happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. It occurred to me that I was surprised that there had not been media use made of the fact that these KLA prisoners were actually extremely reluctant and had been -- had not been described as such, because, in my view, it would have very substantially damaged the Albanian -- the KLA image at the time. But the media at the time, I'm sure you can recall, was that the VJ forces were fighting an implacable enemy rather than these groups of scared boys.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 19, please, the OSCE report for the 13th of January. And we're interested in seeing how things were developing in the Racak area.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: In Stimlje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's on the second page, I think.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I'm having difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Humanitarian activity, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's now being reported --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Pristina Regional Centre visited villages in the Stimlje area following reports that residents had left and taken to the hills. Verifiers found 50 people in Belince, 350 in Racak, and 680 in Malpolje, all of which are in the area around Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did that cause any concern to the OSCE, to have this number of people taking to the hills, or was this standard behaviour of --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was quite normal by this stage that when there was major activity by the Yugoslav forces, that the residents would move out of the area and be given shelter by neighbouring villages. And so this had happened before - it had happened in the summer - and was relatively commonplace. It obviously was of concern because we were talking all the time to the UNHCR, passing this sort of thing on so that they could be helped in providing food relief and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the same page, second line of "Security Situation," we can see a reference to a tank firing 50 to 60 main armament rounds. Again, is that a concerning manner or par for the course?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Well, a tank carries about 40 to 50 rounds in its turret, and so if tanks are firing 50 to 60 rounds, it means that they are doing more than simply responding to a situation with an aimed shot. So again, this indicates to me a very disproportionate response to small-arms fire. Again, one could argue that if you saw exactly where the person was firing at you from and you had a tank available, you might fire one round at that position, but to fire the entire contents of your turret in that direction is very, very disproportionate and would not be allowed in any normal security situation that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraphs 165 and 166. You went, on the 13th of January, to a KLA camp in Stari Trg, waiting for Walker, and held a media conference --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This was in connection with the release of the eight VJ soldiers and really just describes the mechanism by which we were in one place and Walker was in another, with everybody in telephone contact with one another, while the release of the eight VJ soldiers was finalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a reflection of your approach, when the VJ -- the KLA woman, if she was a spokesman or other official, attempted to describe the men as prisoners of war and saying they had been treated correctly, you used different terminology, saying that they were soldiers who had been detained?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't want to find myself being quoted as agreeing that these were prisoners of war, because that would certainly have given a flavour to the conflict that I didn't think was at that stage justified, and so I only referred to them as soldiers who had been detained or held against their will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at paragraph 167, you were able to see that when the soldiers were released, they appeared to have been assaulted, with bruises and black eyes showing --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- terrified of their situation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: They were certainly very frightened, and it was only when we were able to indicate to them that we were -- you know, we were there to take them back that they began to realise that they were not going to get harmed in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Exhibit 20 -- tab 20. I beg your pardon. A substantial OSCE report, of which probably one of the lines we want is unhappily copied in a fold in the paper, but I think you've been able to work out what you think it says in context.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, the summary starts: "It was --" I think: "It was broadly --" or no. I think it's: " ... generally a quiet day."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or evenly "really," I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. "... though there has been much VJ influence on our area of operations because of the Serbian New Year celebrations," I think it is. But I think to see the date on that, which is the 14th of January, and note that we were thinking it was a quiet day, I think indicates that there was not a sort of constant crescendo in the Stimlje and Racak area. Things were happening all over the place that we were responding to, of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which events in Stimlje and Racak were part of, but they were certainly not seen as the main focus of our activity at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 169 and 170 we can perhaps deal with this way: that on the 15th of January, there was a report brought to you in the course of a meeting, about bad things happening in Stimlje. You sent Maisonneuve to investigate and received a report that a KVM member had been wounded in the Decani area, where his vehicle had been fired upon, so you had to go and deal with that as an emergency.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. These were two completely separate incidents, one in the Stimlje area and the other much closer to where we were in Pec, in Decani. And at the time I sent Maisonneuve, whose area Stimlje was not, but it was just over from his area, and so he knew it quite well. So I told him to go and see what was going on in Stimlje, and I went and attempted to sort out the aftermath of having two of our people wounded in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 21, please. Again, this is a one-page document being an OSCE press release dealing with the deliberate shooting at your vehicles at Decani on the 15th of January and setting out how it was that the KLA forces in the area had acknowledged that it was their forces that were responsible for the shooting and the wounding and that it was due to a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This came out sometime later, as you see from the date, 21st of January. At the time that we had our two people wounded, it was not clear who had perpetrated it, and I was very suspicious of everybody at this stage and so was -- was quite convinced it could have been either -- either of the parties in this particular dispute. As a result of a lot of discussion with the Kosovo Liberation Army, they eventually admitted that it was their people, and eventually we then said, "Well, you should admit it publicly," and we gave them a day in which we wanted them to publicly state it, and they did not feel able to do that. And so at that point, we -- we issued a statement in which we said that this had happened, and it was the Kosovo Liberation Army were responsible for it, but it took us five days to track that one down. And of course, while all this was going on, other things were happening elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. 172: On the 15th of January, Ciaglinski and others were having discussion with the MUP in the Decani area.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This was -- this is the detail of the shooting and the wounding of the two verifiers, and I think this -- I think I've covered this in broad detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And 173, we come to Racak itself.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened on the 15th of January was that it appears there was an offensive in the village, and according to you, information coming to you, VJ tanks and Pragas were sighted on the hills around the village.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This was an operation that started in the morning of the 15th and involved firing not only into Racak but into several other villages in the area and consisted at first of tanks and Pragas, which are anti-aircraft artillery which was used in -- heavy anti-aircraft cannon which were used in a ground role and were very rapid firing, being used to fire at Racak and other villages in the area, and it appeared to those who were around and who heard it described that the VJ were firing from the hills, and the police, the MUP, were then going in on foot on the ground. And you can only do this if -- if the people who are going forward are confident that the people who are doing the covering fire are fully aware of your actions on the ground. It does require a very high degree of coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Depending on how time goes, I may ask you to look in due course at a large special map that has been prepared. It may not be a map as much of a photograph, I think, but for the time being, can we look, to deal with things swiftly, at Exhibit 22. Really it's the top left-hand bit of it we need trouble ourselves with, having seen its comparative position in relation to Urosevac. And we can see --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That's Urosevac. That is Stimlje. You can see the two roads joining at Stimlje and then the road going west into the Dulje Heights and on to Suva Reka. The village of Racak is here to the south-west, and the offensive was taking place with the VJ tanks and Pragas firing at this string of villages along the west -- the eastern edge of the high ground that goes away to the west. So the VJ were -- positions were broadly parallel to the main road to the north, and the villages were in a line really north-west to south-east along the edge of the high ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we -- as I say, we may be able to help the Chamber even today with larger scale maps, but we must press on. Having got that general account, reported back to you by Maisonneuve - paragraph 175 - that on his arrival at Racak, he noticed what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Maisonneuve drove straight to Racak, which took him, I suppose, just over an hour from -- from leaving me, and when he got there at the end of the afternoon, he saw that the VJ were withdrawing from the area. So he went into the village, and there he was advised by the villagers that there had been some deaths but it was not specified how many, but it wasn't said that there were a lot, that some people had been arrested and there were a number of wounded people. At that point, he asked what could be done to help the people and was told that it was the wounded who needed looking after, and that was what he got on with as night fell and the light went.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the report of people being arrested, which was in due course to be -- shown to be in complete account of what happened, was that an unusual event?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was not unusual at the time. We on various occasions heard of people being arrested, detained, questioned, and then they would turn up later, having been interrogated to quite a degree in -- in security forces' custody, considerably bruised but certainly alive. So the problem, as he saw it, as he arrived on the Friday evening, was one of wounded people rather than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This we -- or part of this we find reflected, I think, in the next exhibit, which we can look at briefly, tab 23, the OSCE's report of the 15th of January. It deals with the arrested men, I think, or the alleged arrested men.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, I'm -- yes. There we are. Right. I've --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On page 2, I think.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: On page 2, about halfway down, in the middle of the small paragraph, it says that there were five injured, that a female and a young boy were transferred to Stimlje hospital. The KLA spokesman was asked what the OSCE could help to do most and his firm assurance was that they needed -- they needed to know that they could bring in the women and children from the hills, where they had taken refuge, without further VJ attacks that night, and then later that three other wounded civilians were evacuated. If you go back to the front page of this document, you can see the head of RC Prizren comment, that is comment of Maisonneuve, that, "The incident in Stimlje detailed below is a clear breach of the agreement as per our assessment." And that was a very strong statement to come from a Regional Centre head, because I've already mentioned that words of "compliance" and "non-compliance" were reserved very much for the Head of Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same document happens to record the total number of KVM at the time. I think it's probably on the last page, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. It's also of note that one of the patrols on the ground took a statement from a villager who gave him a list of 21 men who had been detained by the MUP and taken to Urosevac gaol. Would you like me to find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Well, not necessarily. It's a repeat, isn't it in?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then don't bother.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It can be found, if necessary. But just as a matter of interest, against the 2.000 mandated KVM manpower force, by this time I think we can work out it's about 854 is the number you derive as being there at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Sorry, can I see that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the last page.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: There was always two figures. Yes. One was -- no, it's the one before. That's personnel status. No. That's -- no, that's Regional Centre Prizren. That's Regional Centre Prizren personnel, which is 285, rather than the total strength of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be in here somewhere, but perhaps you can help us. Were you remotely up to full strength by that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Sorry, I think that is -- I think what we've got is -- you're referring to the next document in which is the report from Pristina, from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: -- the head of the OSCE, in which we stated ourselves as being 854 strong at that moment. Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The -- you've referred to the strength of opinion expressed in these reports. Becoming concerned at what you were learning about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: At this stage, it was serious, but it was not the most serious thing that we felt we had faced, and so I think that was reflected in the reports that were put together overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So we come to Exhibit 24, OTP reference 1598.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: And this is the report that would have been compiled late on the Friday evening, after the reports from the Regional Centres had been received, and that would be sometime after 9.00 at night, and then we would send it up to Vienna in the early hours of the morning. And so this is really our perception around about midnight in Pristina. And it is, I think, worthy of note that we were trying to stick to the facts that we knew rather than -- rather than speculate, because we often found that the first report could be exaggerated. So it was better only to stick to what you really knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So on page 2, paragraph 4, where you deal with what's coming out of Racak, it says, "Verifiers saw," third line --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- "one dead Albanian civilian and five injured civilians."

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. "The KVM also received unconfirmed reports of other deaths in the area. Residents claim that the men had been segregated from the women and -- from the women and children and that 20 males had been arrested. This remains unconfirmed." So there was, as I say, great stress in sticking to what we really knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: But you can see further down that we witnessed VJ tanks and armoured vehicles firing directly into houses near Malpolje and Petrova, again villages in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document - my mistake - sets out your international staff --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- of 854 against the mandated 2.000.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. And that really sort of, I think, indicates that there we were, three months into a 12-month mission, and we were still not yet at half of our mandated strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And since your evidence is, we hope, going to give an account of the developing picture, can we now look at another document of the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder if that would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. Would you be back, please, General, at half past two. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, Exhibit tab -- start again. Tab 25, OTP reference 1602. Now, this is, I think, an example of an OSCE morning situation brief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That is correct. This is the brief that was given at 9.00 to the Head of Mission on the morning of Saturday, the 16th of January. So this is what we were -- what we had distilled as the mission's official view of the situation as at the start of that Saturday morning. It's perhaps worthy of note that there's more than one entry on this, and so it was seen as being the morning after a difficult day, when a number of things were going on, all of which were quite important. It was not at this stage seen that Racak was by far the most important event going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Now, just look at the format of it. It comes in several pages. You have the map with the identified problem areas, significant events, as reported on a few following pages.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: And then on each page afterwards, the particular serial of the box on the main map, there is the text of the words that we used for briefing. If we go to number 5, you can see the description that was used at the time that the attack had started in the vicinity of Stimlje at approximately 7.00. "Racak and three other villages came under attack. The fighting and shelling were heavy throughout the day, and this attack follows the build-up in the area which occurred last week, after the KLA ambushed a MUP patrol. It's expected this battle will continue tomorrow. KVM patrols are for the most part being denied access to the battle area."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's also a reference to Racak on number 4, Prizren. There's reference to the battle in the area of Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This was to do with the rotation of police, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. The concern there was whether or not police were being moved to reinforce in the Stimlje area or whether this was a normal changeover of people, because the police stations tended to be manned on a continuous basis by the same crew for a number of days and then they would be rotated; they would be changed with another lot who would come in and the original ones would go off for a rest. So that's the point behind that entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think you had a conversation --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Late on the Friday night, I was attempting to phone General Loncar, couldn't get him, and got Colonel Kotur instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 26. Is this the one?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. And in this -- in the middle of a note of -- and I think this is a -- I know this is a record of what I said that was taken down by one of the people with me at the time, saying: "The second area I'm concerned about is Stimlje. We're hearing alarming reports of anti-aircraft artillery being used in the ground role and being directed into villages. This is not police action, as we understand it. This is very close to the sort of action that was so bad in the summer." That's referring to 1998. "This sort of action must cease immediately. You are to pass this message from me to the top of your chain of command. The operations in these areas must be ordered to cease immediately. Firing anti-aircraft weapons into villages with women and children in them is not police action. This must be ordered to stop. Ambassador Walker will be contacting your superiors tomorrow, after I have briefed him on this conversation that I am having with you now at 2320, on the 15th of January."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: -- these things as they were beginning to unfold might well need to be officially recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, you're being asked to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What we've seen over the recent bits of evidence and exhibits, that your mission was cautious in its approach, mindful of its experience that reports were sometimes initially worse than reality, even if this was one which was going to turn out to be the reverse.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Correct. We were, I think, very -- very conscious that you can sometimes make a situation worse by overreacting to -- to an initial -- an initial report. And there had been instances of that certainly in December of 1998 when alarming reports came in which, upon investigation, were less awful than the first report. And we had spent a lot of time stressing to our people on the ground to report the facts and only what they saw. And if someone rushed up to them and said, "Something awful has happened," to make sure that they were reporting it as something that had been told them and distinguish between that and what they had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on. Paragraph 180. On the 16th of January, were you getting reports of more casualties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. The reports started to come in as we -- as we started the day on the 16th, that the situation at Racak was indeed worse than we had first thought. Each of these reports on its own was not in itself an immediate trigger to action, but the fact that they were coming in from so many different sources and appeared to be independent was clearly very worrying. And simultaneously, the situation over in the west at Decani was also hotting up, was also becoming a problem again, and exchanges of fire were being reported. And so we appeared to have two separate bad situations at the beginning of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to deal with paragraph 181, but if you can get the heart of it out quite shortly. This is 11.15 in the morning of the 16th, and you have a conversation with Ciaglinski and Loncar.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The topic is Decani, Racak, and Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: At this time, I walked over to General Loncar's office with Richard Ciaglinski, and I had, in setting up the meeting, indicated that I wanted to talk about the three issues. And literally as we were starting to walk out of our building on the walk across to General Loncar's building, we were getting more and more reports that indicated that it was Racak that was the really big problem. I was still concerned about Decani, because it was there that we had had our two people wounded, and I was of the opinion at that stage that these people had been wounded by the -- by the Serbian police and that this had been an attempt to -- to wrongly implicate the KLA. This was a wrong view, as we eventually found out, but that was my view at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You challenged Loncar, and that was what? With the Decani matter rather than with anything else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No. We started off on Decani, but we quite quickly moved on to Racak. As I indicated, we had -- we had started to get these extra reports in, and so I said, "I need to talk about what is going on at Racak," and he assumed an air of innocence and was extremely cool in the way he dealt with this, which was not the normal way he dealt with things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, I think, said to him or he read your comments as allegations of knowledge and he said, "Who, us? No way."

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, or similar words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To which you replied?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: To which I replied, "Look, this sort of behaviour is the way that people end up in The Hague." He was quite angry and said, "How dare you. How dare you say that to me." And I said, "Look, you know, this is getting really serious, and this is the way it is going. You need to understand this."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So let's look at tab 27. OSCE report. And it's -- deals with Decani.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It deals with a meeting involving Loncar and yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: If we go down to Stimlje, at paragraph 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There it sets out how you explain --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- how you and Walker were going to investigate and that, "The next stop for your people will be in The Hague."

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I stated that reports had been received from the villages of the killings of, and at this stage I described it as women, children, and old men. I said on behalf of Walker, because Walker had made it clear that I was to adopt an extremely uncompromising attitude in this matter, I said that he and I were going down to look at this personally, and again this is recorded as, "The next step for your people will be The Hague." If those are not the words, they're very close to the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: And over the page, the top of the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We can read it, actually, fairly swiftly. You said that -- he said --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Loncar said that we shouldn't refer to regular police work as provocative. I came back and said that, "This is not regular police work, firing anti-aircraft cannon into villages." And -- and he then stated that what had happened at Decani when we'd got our guys or when our guys had been wounded was as a result of ourselves setting it up, to which I responded quite vigorously. And we then discussed the various versions of the -- of the events. At this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You indicated at paragraph 7 that you were going to Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had verified that there was no more -- there was more provocative action in Decani, which was stopped, that the situation wasn't helped by force around Podujevo, and you reminded the general of the statement he made that if the VJ prisoners were released, the troops would return to barracks. The VJ prisoners had, of course, now been released, and they hadn't gone back to barracks.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. That was the firm impression we had got at the end of the situation, which was only a couple of days earlier where we had got the people off the top of the mountain, that this was then going to be allowed to calm down and that troops would be returned to barracks. And obviously this had not happened in that on the Friday there had been this action in the Stimlje-Racak area. And so again I went through the formula of how many forces were allowed out of barracks and how many were out of barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to have to move fairly swiftly, General. I think that you also dealt with the disproportionality and inappropriateness --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- of using anti-aircraft cannon in an internal security situation. So if we just look at the other side -- not the other side, because they weren't another side, but the other side of this meeting's record of it. It's tab 28, a document you've only seen very recently.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your view, I think, expressed in paragraph 183, is that it mixes up events of Decani with those of Stimlje and Racak.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that this happened because the person who was acting as the secretary and signs the document is not the guy who normally did it, and I'm pretty sure that the normal supporting people who General Loncar normally had were not all there at this meeting, because this meeting was called at short notice, was not a pre-arranged meeting in the normal course of events, and so there's evidence of mix-up in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the foot of the first page and beginning of the second, we can see you adopting a harsh approach, according to Loncar's notetaker: "Attempting to make points he wished to make to General Loncar, one by one, as urgently as possible, endeavouring in this manner to prevent our side from setting out our own arguments and facts." Just pausing there for a minute, of course in looking at the other side of the meeting's records and looking at the VJ's record of events, we'll be interested to see if there is, in fact, any contemporaneous account of what happened at Racak.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. As I recall it, I don't think there is a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So they go on in their record to note that: "With respect to the note which General Loncar sent to Walker, asking the KVM members to secure the return of weapons," and so on, "General Drewienkiewicz said he had no intention of exposing the lives of his verifiers to danger." And then a demand that army members be withdrawn from Podujevo. Then a demand that operations about Decani be halted. Then a reference to the two injured or wounded KVM members, you saying you didn't know who the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. perpetrator was. Then focusing on the operation in the area of Stimlje. It records your information that civilians, including children, women, and the elderly, had been killed, and saying that you were going to go to the scene, as indeed you were. And then at the next page, saying that it would be bad for your side.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A summary of Loncar's position being that your approach was tendentious - paragraph 3 - that your decision to go with journalists reflected bias and that it would be more appropriate if an investigation was carried out first and journalists summoned subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This simply didn't -- this is what was said, and that situation was really not a feasible suggestion in that obviously we didn't control where the journalists were going. It was clear that the journalists had decided they were going to go to this area, irrespective of anything we did. My point was as much that it was important that General Loncar accompanied us so that he could agree with us what was there rather than having to rely on reports at secondhand through the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in the event, did he come with you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: He didn't come with us, in the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see at the bottom of the page you were said to have been visibly nervous, refusing coffee, that you calmed down. Were you nervous or angry?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I was extremely angry. I certainly did refuse coffee and was well aware that that would give an indication of the fact that I was more -- very much more serious than perhaps was normally the case, that this was so serious that I was not prepared to sit down and drink coffee while this situation was evolving.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You observe, in paragraph 183, that there were less than the normal number of copies of this particular document made. Any significance in that, or is that just --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think it reflects the fact that the normal secretariat people were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: But also that less copies were made, and therefore this report was sent to less people, which would suggest that there was a feeling of sensitivity about it, because if you want to restrict the distribution of it, you obviously make less copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As we can see, the document contains no narrative account from the Serb side --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- of what had happened. So if we move on from that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- when you are dealing with these kind of documents, written in Serb and which were not brought by this witness, could you clarify to us how or where you did get these kind of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. These documents came -- [Microphone not activated] -- being produced --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Turn on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's on already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't immediately give you the precise source of this document. I'll do so in due course. But they generally have come to us from sources, the providence of which will be satisfactory, and you can see indeed that they're stamped and signed and everything else. I can't immediately tell you where that one came from, but I will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or probably Ms. Graham, with her access to the records, will be able to tell me in the blink of an eye, I expect. It will take a few more moments than that. I'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to the next exhibit, the next tab in the exhibit, tab 29. This is an OSCE document on the 16th of January. General, any particular significance in this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think this is -- may I quickly look at it and refresh my memory again? This is our -- is my secretary's -- or my staff officer's version of what -- of the meeting that we have just heard described from the Serbian perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We needn't trouble with it any more, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: And I think I've covered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you had explained you were going to travel to Racak, that Loncar, whatever his initial reaction, in the event, did not go with you. When you arrived - paragraph 185 - at Racak, was there already a substantial presence of other people there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. We drove through Stimlje, where there were a lot of Serbian police, and then driving from Stimlje the one and a half kilometres down to Racak, there was a considerable media presence of the international media. There were no Serbian forces in the village of Racak. There were a number of KLA people there, seven or eight of them, I recall, spread out just throughout the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have drawn a map, but I've now been able to obtain reduced-size prints of aerial photographs. Which do you think would be more helpful to explain the geography?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think the aerial photo is rather better than my rather scruffy print.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These have been distributed in colour, by another reference, to the amici and to the accused earlier. There are two colour copies. Why don't I make one of my colour copies available, my colour copy. Is that -- no, I'll have to keep one back. There are two colour copies and several black-and-white ones for distribution. And if the tab numberings on this exhibit reach number -- I think it's up to 71, or is it 72? 72. And this becomes tab 73 of this binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know, General, that you've recently seen this map, which is part of the production of another witness yet to come, so that the markings on it - and it's a display map - are not what we are particularly interested in. It's just the map for its own value at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are the two. There's the smaller sheet -- three, actually. There's the general aerial view, which shows the whole area. And perhaps you'll just acquaint the Judges, and others watching, with the general geography by reference to this one first. If we could lay that on the ELMO, and then we'll go to the detailed maps. If you can just explain the route, the arrival, and where the village is. Then we'll see it on the other maps in more detail.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Right. This road is the main road that goes up into the Dulje Heights. That's the town of Stimlje. And from Stimlje, the road into Racak is down this way, and Racak is in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on, the mental hospital to which you've made reference, can you find that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Is about there. Sorry, probably about there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, with that, we can probably move immediately to the slightly larger-scale map, forgetting the markings that relate to the work of another witness to come.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Which one do you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first one, the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Is that Racak or the municipality of Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The municipality of Stimlje, I think. Just lay that there and we can see it in a little more detail, and then we can go to the largest scale of all. So this shows, if we can just see the road in --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Right. The red circles represent the positions from which fire was brought into Racak. That's particularly this ridge, which faces west, and Racak is in this area. You can see it spread out astride this road. And the marking which is shown as "6," which is there, is the ravine up which we went. So to get into the village, we came in along this road, parked up pretty well on that corner, and then were led up a ravine to the point that's marked as "6."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now I'll move to the largest-scale map of all, part of the same tab number, Racak itself. Not map; aerial view. That shows the road in, the ridge still marked in red. And can you now, by leaving that on the ELMO, can you pick up your narrative? You arrived at the village.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Right. And we --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The KLA people, where were they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: They were scattered throughout the village. There were a couple at the entry to the village, at the eastern edge of the village, which I suppose is down south of the area where the mosque is shown. There's the mosque. So the entrance to the village is round about here. So we saw a couple here, and then as we went into the village, along this fairly straight piece of road there were three or four, visibly in uniform, standing around with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The point you've just indicated, there is another road or roadway or track going off to the right, but that apart, that appears to be only the one road into Racak. What is the position? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The road into Racak that vehicles used was the one that came down here and turned right and then came in this way. This road is a lot less distinct on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you arrived -- I'm sorry. I'm going too fast. When you arrived at the village, the first sign of what had happened is, I think, the body of a man in a farmhouse.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just can you point that area to us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That would be in about this area. It was just after this corner. We were taken into the courtyard, and the body was lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The body being the body of what and in what state?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The body of an elderly man who had had his head chopped off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then did you return to the village or to another part of the village where you noticed a newly dug trench system?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We moved on westwards from this corner to the up -- starting to go up the hill, and where the hill became wooded, there was a trench system which was at least 50 metres long which faced east. In other words, it was about a semi-circle like this, facing in this and this direction, covering the open ground to the -- to the north of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We may, if the video that's being produced works on the machine here, which it didn't on the one I was trying to work it on at lunchtime, see a video which shows that trench system, but I think your recollection and note of it was that it was newly-built and unused for reasons you can give.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I did take some notes of this, thinking that this might have been an area where there had been fighting. If there had been fighting, then there would almost certainly have been spent cartridge cases and other evidence of it having been occupied. Cigarette papers, cigarette butts, anything like that; the normal litter of a battlefield. You know, clips that ammunition had been in, discarded bits of uniform --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: -- and there was none of that. It was very, very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't want the video yet. Thank you. But we'll come to it in a second. Thank you for turning it off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it was my conclusion that this trench had not been fought over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any scenes of crime examination being done at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No. We did not have those sort of specialists in the mission. However, partly because of that, the instruction was given to our -- one of our photographers to video everything he saw in as much detail as he could, which he then did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just tell us, before we turn over from tab 30, which is probably redundant in light of the aerial views, was tab 30 the map or plan you drew at the time or later?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That was later. I didn't draw a sketch at the time. This was drawn in June of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
