utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were there with Ambassador Walker and the press. Their pressure was what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: There was a lot -- the press were obviously taking their photos and were hounding Walker to make a statement. He moved around the scene, noted what had been seen and then did make a statement at the time. But it was really quite factual at the time, and no attribution of what had happened was given at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, at the moment, have only told us of seeing the one decapitated elderly man. I'm going to ask you in a minute to talk us through a little bit more of what you saw, but what was the attitude of the villagers, the surviving villagers in the village, generally?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: They appeared to be extremely shocked and in considerable fear and trepidation. We got, I got, the impression that the KLA were not welcome in the village, that they had imposed themselves upon the village rather than being there and being made welcome. There were no signs that the KLA were in any way welcome in this village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There were KLA present?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there were villagers present?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were able to see the interaction of one to the other?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: They were not talking to one another, chatting, exchanging cigarettes or anything like that. There was -- they were avoiding each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you -- did you take from any villagers an account - just yes or no at this stage - of what the KLA had done the previous day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The account, and I can't remember exactly how I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It sounds as though the answer to my question was yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this was through an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it was from one or more than one of the villagers, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was from more than one because it was largely when we were standing around after we'd been on the hill, and we were using the interpreter of the UNHCR official who was there. And we were chatting to a number of the people who were there, who were coming up to us to offer their versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what, if there was any consistency in the version advanced, was the account of what the KLA had done?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The consistent account was that the KLA had essentially left the village when the Serb forces had come into the village, that they had not stopped and fought. And there was a degree of bitterness among the villagers that the KLA had stayed there long enough to make trouble but not long enough to do anything about it when -- when trouble came in the other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It might now be convenient to look at the video. The whole video, Your Honour, is a 30-minute video. The extracts are half a minute or something of that extent, I think. For technical reasons, I wasn't able to view the extract that's been prepared, although I have seen parts of it with the witness before. It's Exhibit number -- does it have a separate exhibit number or is it part of this binder? May it have a new exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's proposed, and I hope this is acceptable, if the full tape could be produced as 95. The extract which we will play to save time can be 95A, and people can view the whole hand-held video at their leisure if they wish to. So if the extract can now be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, either speak over it as we see it, although much of it speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This is us arriving, coming up the hill through the orchard to the point where the trench is, and I think we then see ourselves crossing the trench. We see our feet going across the trench. But you can see the way that this area looks out over -- over open countryside. You can also see the effects of Serb artillery on the houses in the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's, I think, you there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I'm in the yellow anorak. Walker is just turning towards us in the blue anorak, with the moustache and glasses. Now this is us coming up to the trench system and crossing the trench system. I mean, it is a trench running from left to right as we crossed it. And then we're going up the hill towards the ravine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, from what you've been told, you've already been told what to expect in the ravine, presumably?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. We knew that there were a number of bodies up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the original video show the bodies as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I believe -- yes, it did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe we'll make another part of it available tomorrow. But in any event, that's going to be evidenced in another place at another time. But when you got to the trench at the top, what was it that you found? Not the trench, the ravine.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We went up the hill through -- along a -- what became a path with a -- with a wall on either side. And then as that levelled out towards the top of the hill, it became more open, and at that point we came across -- it really turned into the gulley in which we came across the bodies of 24 men. They had all been shot, and it was my impression that most had been shot in the upper part of the body, in the head and neck. All were wearing civilian clothing. There was no evidence of any uniforms and no evidence of any weapons. In the gulley itself there was nothing to indicate fighting, such as spent cartridge cases. Most of the ones I saw were elderly rather than young. I thought at the time they were 50 to 60, but they might have been younger, a bit younger, because -- but they were certainly not young men. They were more than 40, say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now just deal with a couple of exhibits before we come to the evening press conference.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Could I also add that their footwear and their clothing was not the sort of footwear and clothing that I associate with people who live in the hills. They were wearing wellingtons and mackintosh sort of garments rather than the sort of things you would wear if you were living in the hills. Several of them were also wearing the white cap, which again was not something that we had noticeably seen in our visits to KLA locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go to tab 31, please. OTP reference 1558, a press article detailing the casualties for the 8th to the 20th of January. And we can see this in its original form in the publication of a newspaper, I think.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- of this please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is a statement of what the police casualties were over this period, and I think it's a translation of a newspaper article. The -- and the period covered is the 8th to the 20th of January, which of course includes Racak which was on the 15th. And if you go through the -- the dates on which the report indicates, it appears that one police officer was wounded on the 15th of January and none were reported killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's on the second sheet, isn't it, the top of the second sheet?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, it is. "The officer who was born in 1969 was slightly wounded in a terrorist attack committed near the village of Racak on the 15th of January." Now, it therefore appears that while 45 Albanians were killed and five were wounded, one Serbian policeman was wounded, which again hardly indicates a firefight in which the fire was moving in both directions. It indicates to me that the fire was -- was exclusively being directed at the Albanians. If the people on the hillside at Racak had been resisting, then I believe that more than one person would have ended up wounded. More than one policeman would have ended up wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I gather I was too impatient with the video extract, and if we had waited a little bit longer we would have gone from pure blue back to the next passage. So if it's still in the same position -- I see a positive sign -- we can just play the next bit. I gather that -- ah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, is this in the ravine or is this somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This is moving uphill, up the ravine. And we started seeing one or two individuals on their own and then we came across a group, a larger group of people who were -- who had fallen, who were heaped on one another. That's Walker there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Walker in the blue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: In the blue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made the observation about the footwear.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. And here is the heap, yes, one of the heaps of bodies which appear to be where they fell. And we could detect no sign of them having been moved around. And similarly, we could see no evidence that clothing had been removed. They appeared to have the bullet holes in the clothing that were consistent with the wounds. Again, if you're going to run around the hills, then these light-coloured anoraks are not the thing to wear because you obviously show up in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed were there any signs of resistance or fighting, or defence --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: None whatsoever that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- where these men had fallen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: There were no indications that they had fought back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's probably all. There's nothing we've now missed, is there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I don't think there is, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much to the audiovisual unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on to tab 32, just the contemporaneous record, your own OSCE report. Marked at "C" is your -- I think this is your record, is it, or record of somebody on the same team?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Sorry, can I look? The paragraph marked "C" at the bottom of the first page exactly describes what I saw. I don't think it was necessarily drafted by me, because this was something that was written I think two or three days later as a formal report to Vienna and again was an attempt to be absolutely specific on the facts as opposed to the press reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see a reference there to one of the men shot in the head, having a wound which had scorch marks around it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I did not see that, but that is as a result of putting together everybody's -- everybody's recollection of what they saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the conclusion says -- speaks of execution.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. That's the top of the next page, isn't it? "Observations recorded in the details in group C led the KVM to the conclusion that the civilians had obviously been executed. The KVM described these observations as a massacre and attributed responsibility to the FRY government security forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you returned to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. We moved back down the hill and then Walker was then asked to go and talk to the -- those of the village elders that were left, and went and did that on his own. At this stage, the rest of us were prevented from leaving, and this is when we stood around and talked with those villagers who came up and were willing to talk to us. And then we then all left the village together. I rode back with Walker, and in the vehicle, we agreed that there would be -- he directed that there would be a further press conference that evening in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe before we get to the press conference, it's not covered, in fact, in the printed statement, but there's been some reference in these proceedings to phone calls made at the time by individuals who were there, on mobile phones. Just help us with that, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. There was some mobile phone activity from the -- the area at the top of the hill. I specifically remember the aide of Walker making a phone call. I cannot remember to whom he made it. The mobile phone reception in that area was not good, and so not that many were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make any?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I don't recall doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you in a position to help us - yes or no - with the content of anybody else's phone call?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think that -- I think that Walker's assistant was phoning through to NATO at the time. I'm pretty sure there was an American at the other end of it. I'm not specifically sure who he did speak to, but he basically was describing the scene on the hillside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on, then, to the press conference. How was that dealt with? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We then went back to Pristina. Walker had spoken to the press on the hillside, had confined himself very much to describing the facts as he had seen them on the hillside, and then we went back to Pristina and arranged a subsequent press conference. And over the course of the time between getting back to Pristina and having the press conference, a number of us did phone back to capitals in order to report that something really bad had happened. I certainly at that stage rang through to London and said that something really bad had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware of anybody else's phone calls?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I reported to Walker that the press conference had been laid on as he had instructed it, and when I walked into his office, he was on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear his phone call?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think he was on the phone to Richard Holbrooke, because his exact words that I recall where, "Dick, you can kiss your Nobel Peace Prize goodbye."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The press conference itself, was that notable for some attribution of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. At the press conference, either in the original statement or I think in response to questions afterwards, Walker said yes, he believed this was a massacre, and yes, he believed that the Yugoslav security forces were responsible for the killings. So he did at that point directly attribute the blame to the Yugoslav security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Loncar had not accompanied you on this journey, despite having once said he would. Did you have contact with him on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. He actually came across to my office and said he needed to talk about this, that he was -- he had just heard of the content of the press conference and that he felt it was not -- had not been done properly, that he had been instructed by Belgrade to come over and to deliver this message. He made the point strongly that Walker had not made the point in his press conference that everything that had happened at Racak had been in response to the earlier murder of the three policemen, that everything that had gone on in Racak was because police had gone into Racak searching for the people who had killed the police a week earlier. And it was that point he was wishing to make at that stage rather than saying what had happened at Racak in the previous 24 hours. He was more intent on justifying the presence of Yugoslav security forces in the village rather than commenting on what had actually happened, whether it was in response to orders or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 33. This is a press statement. Before we come to that: His Honour Judge Kwon's inquiry, I do have an answer, but there are certain sensitivities concerned. Can I give you a detailed answer tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 33 is a statement from the press. Your comment coming on --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, it's a statement that originated on the 16th, despite the fact that it says the 14th of January, because you can read in the detail that it's all about yesterday, the 15th of January. It is the statement from the -- I think the FRY authorities and was put together after the evening press conference by Walker in Pristina, which I recall happening starting around 6.00 and which lasted about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, we don't want to take time reading documents in detail. We can scan-read them ourselves. The significance for you of this document being what, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think it states -- it is very anti-Walker. It states of what Walker did and talking about the competent judicial authorities carrying out their legal obligations. It does not actually state what -- the degree of the killing. It does not state that 40-something people had been killed there. And I think that is remarkable, when lists of injured policemen can be produced, that an incident in which 46 Kosovar Albanians are killed is not worthy of note.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see in the first paragraph the summary explanation for the event being police undertaking to arrest terrorists who killed a police officer in a terrorist attack.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And again, the statement that the terrorists attacked them with automatic weapons, portable launchers, and mortars is at odds with what I saw on the ground and what had been reported earlier as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 34. And His Honour Judge Kwon's query reminds me that I've been, in the interests of brevity, deviating from my normal practice of asking that the original first be laid on the ELMO so that those viewing can see the nature of the original document. So can it briefly be -- can you place the B/C/S original on the overhead projector briefly first so that people can see the nature of the document, and then we'll look at the English version. And while that's being done -- there's the original document. We can now replace that with the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does this appear to be a record from the FRY of the meeting between --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- yourself and Loncar, a document you hadn't seen until very recently?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That's correct. I saw this again just before Easter. It reminds me that General Loncar, having come first to my office, we then walked together down to Walker's office and there was then a continuation of the discussion, in which Loncar had protested what Walker had said at the press conference. And I think we have some words -- Loncar said on this occasion he was submitting an official report on the given incident and he had to express his surprise that we had already transmitted to the media our perception of events, which was, to say the least, neither complete nor credible. This evening's presentation by the Head of Mission at a press conference, where a biased perception of the incident was presented. Highly inappropriate that no reference was made to the fact that our side - which is the Serbian side - had invited the KVM to verify the need it undertook towards killing on 10th January, being the killing of the policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Too fast, I suspect, General.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Sorry. That it made no reference to the fact that the Serb authorities had invited the KVM to verify the killings of the policeman on the 10th of January. And he goes on, you can see at the bottom of the page: "The incident had practically occurred because of the organised actions of the terrorists against the activity of the police," and claiming that this had been a scenario prepared in advance for the benefit of the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's fair to observe, at the bottom of the third page and over to the fourth, that it sets out how Walker, following interjections, was steadfast in his thesis that it was a matter of the plain execution of elderly people and civilians who were killed by close-range fire, a clear-cut case which The Hague Tribunal needed to get involved in. It goes on to deal with the information provided to governments of other countries.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. And at this stage and at other stages, Walker had made the strong point that the representatives of this Tribunal should be immediately given entry visas so that they could see the facts on the ground for themselves, and of course that was never followed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And again, apart from the very cursory -- that's a matter for comment. Apart from the explanations thus far given, no detailed account of what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That is correct. No detailed account of what happened was ever given, nor was any response ever given to the suggestion that there should be a proper investigation that commanders who were involved should be suspended during this investigation that was being recommended. All of this was ignored.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exhibit, 35. Your Honours, the same query as to providence of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably the same answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the morning brief --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm addressing His Honour at the moment. The providence of this document, probably the same answer as the previous one. I'll deal with it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then see a document, the appearance of which is already familiar because it is distinctive, and so this is the morning briefing the following day, the 17th of January.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I was not actually in the headquarters at this stage, but I know that this is the briefing that was given. I had already left that morning for Stimlje. But I think the facts are outlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you just find the ...

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It's number -- it's labelled on the front as number 4. It's actually number 3, which says: "EU-KDOM reported a large number of local civilians. Approximately 45 had been killed in the vicinity of Racak. A majority of them appeared to be non-combatants. Loncar was informed of these slayings directly by Walker. Survivors --" and this is other reports that I did not myself participate in -- "reported that they had recognised Serb civilians from the Stimlje area dressed as MUP and other local MUP participating in the killings. They further reported that others described as VJ dressed in black and wearing ski masks over their faces were also involved." That statement, starting with "survivors," is something which I am aware of but no -- I am not -- I have never taken part in any of those conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to the very end of this little clutch of papers, where the type size changes or --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Assessment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see again -- will this be a composite assessment made by the reporting officer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. The last sentence, I think, "Movement of forces might only be a further [sic] step if further forces are needed in the vicinity of Stimlje." So this was showing the way troops were being moved within Kosovo, and I think indicates still that bad though Stimlje was, and Racak was, there was a lot of other stuff going on at the time. This was not one isolated incident in an otherwise calm situation, that there was a lot of other movement in other areas that was needing to be watched and reported on as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one comment there. The assessment, if you could help us, General, assessment for 17th of January, page K0223030 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bias --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- begins, if I could just put it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Begins: "The area around Stimlje is red hot." It then deals with the bodies in Racak. "Expected that the KLA will retaliate. The apparent massacre has the indications that the Serbian civilians could have been involved. Professional soldiers or MUP forces would not normally conduct such atrocities, given the Charter agreements which has involved OSCE in Kosovo. Consequently, the sighting of Serbian civilians by villagers suggest they could very well be responsible, for they are not controlled by the government." Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was, I would say, the first attempt to assess it, and in this case, I have to say, was using reports which were not -- this was not all of the facts. There was a degree of speculation in this, and that speculation was not borne out by anything we were able to find subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As an assessment, it -- in the assessment, it's really what the briefer feels at the time and what could happen. And so it is -- there is a degree of speculation in that, because he is trying to look forward, to say: So what's going to happen next? And so whereas everything else that you have seen is factual, in the assessment the briefer would, as I say, attempt to look forward and see what the implications of the report that he's just given might be in trying to direct the attention of the Head of Mission to the next place where his presence might be needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraphs 202 and onwards, but we'll deal with them very shortly, I think. You went to Stimlje on the 17th of January, having positioned Maisonneuve in the village of Racak for monitoring purpose. You went to the police station and met Bogoljob Janicjevic, and also a woman judge, Danica Marinkovic, from Pristina; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. This meeting was agreed at the Loncar meeting the evening before, when Loncar said, "Look, we still have to get in and carry out the legal obligations here." And it was agreed that I should make contact with the people that needed to go in, in an attempt to keep the situation from bubbling over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about the reaction and approach of the woman judge.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Her view was that she needed to go in with as many police as it needed to ensure her safety. My point was that she would be a lot safer if she went in with us and without a large police presence, because I felt that, in the light of what had just happened, a large police presence was more likely to be provocative than anything, and she didn't need a police presence, in my view, if we were there to guarantee her safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did she heed your advice about the potentially provocative nature of a large police presence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No. And when I became more specific and said, "Look, if you go in with police, you are not only going to be unsafe yourself, you're going to restart the cycle of violence and there will be more trouble and more people will get hurt," and she said, "Well, in that case, so be it." By this stage, I had actually got my people in the village as well, and I said, "Look, if you are absolutely determined to go into this village with a heavy police presence, you must, at the very least, before you start that, give me time to withdraw my people, because I know that if you do that, there is likely to be an exchange of fire." And she eventually gave the order to the police commander in the room with us to give the order that they were to go forward to the village, and at that point I literally had to turn to Ciaglinski and tell him to use his radio to tell everybody to get out, which they then did. And there was no time given even for my people to get clear of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that your advice was rather borne out by events, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: She went to the village. There was a firefight, because the KLA were back in the village in some numbers. And as a result of that, she was not able to go into the village, and I think one of the vehicles with her was actually hit by a rocket-propelled grenade, and so they then came back and had another go the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 36, please. The 18th of January.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is the Yugoslav government's statement, in which Walker was declared persona non grata and was ordered to leave within 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And apart from that, it also makes observations about this Tribunal having no jurisdiction on Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Indeed, yes. Not a view I shared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. We move on to 37, daily report for the 18th of January.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think the point of this report, which comes from Orahovac, is that there was an attempt not to be completely obsessed with what was going on here, that there was -- it was important that throughout the rest of the area, the KVM continued to operate as normally as possible, because it was clearly important that the reporting continued for as long as we were able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Something I haven't covered. It's probably obvious taken as read and visible from the video. The OSCE were unarmed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Completely?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And although some of your vehicles may have, at some stages, had light protection --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The vehicles --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- best you could offer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The vehicles we had were a mix of Pajeros, which were just commercial Pajeros, and some jeeps which had a bit of extra protection, which we laughingly called armoured, but they actually had hardened glass, which slowed a bullet down but which did not stop it, and slightly more robust doors. So they were not armoured vehicles in the way you might think of them. They were certainly not aggressive-looking vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 38, please. Please place the original first on the overhead projector so that it can be viewed, and then we'll look at the English. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This, General, being --?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is the FRY version of a subsequent meeting between General Loncar and myself on the 19th of January, which of course is two days after the Sunday in which the investigating judge and I had sat in Stimlje and discussed whether or not she should go forward with one policeman or a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can see on the foot of the first page in the translation, at number 2, your narrative of what had happened with Judge Danica Marinkovic, and that goes on to page 2.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. And my point here was that this was just increasing the level of violence and went through in great detail because it was the -- it had become the norm in these meetings to go through the detail because attempts to describe things in general terms had very early on been rubbished and details was always required by -- by General Loncar and his people. So one always went in there with a chapter and verse ready to be absolutely specific. It was not good enough to say, you know, "Please stop your people from looting." We had to say, "Please stop your people from looting such as happened on last Wednesday at this place with these people." There was always a great demand for detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see on the third page, at 3.1, reference not only to Walker's persona non grata declared status but the welcome or otherwise extended to Justice Louise Arbour, the Prosecutor at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. The purpose of the whole meeting was to attempt to find out what were the possible intentions of the Yugoslav government with regard to Walker, because obviously his declaration of being persona non grata had a pretty dramatic effect upon the ability of the mission to carry out its job. There was concern that Walker was only the first name at the top of the list and that other people were on this list, and that also that because Walker had resolved to stay put in Pristina, that there might be a storming of the -- of the KVM premises in order to apprehend him, which was at the time thought to be a possibility by some of the people. And so it was seen as quite important to attempt to find out what the likely intentions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the next page we can a see a reference to the IRA and the KLA as a discussion topic. I think that's something that happened quite regularly, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. That was certainly a parallel that was drawn that we -- we -- this was in the context of not -- not honouring the KLA with the word of "army." And I said, "Well, in our operations in Northern Ireland, one of the things that worried us least was what they were called." But it was often brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any detailed account given as to how all these people had died?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we come to 30 -- so sorry. I think on the 21st of January, Ambassador Walker spoke to you following a meeting with Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This was a phone call, and in the course of this phone call Walker reported or said to me that Sainovic had informed him of what he described as the successful outcome of the Racak operation in the afternoon of the 15th of January. So again, at this stage there was no indication from the Yugoslav government side that something really, really bad had happened, that something had happened which was reprehensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thirty-nine, which is OTP reference 2800, a report of yours through the period up to the 19th of January.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This again gives details of -- of incidents happening elsewhere in Kosovo, including a combined VJ and MUP operation in the Glogovac area, which is roughly in the middle of Kosovo. And again, this sort of level of violence that is being reported is, I would say, typical of what was going on round about then. So again, it wasn't just Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forty. I'm passing over some meetings and journeys that you made --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- just to look at the general picture really. 28th of January report, and this, I think, draws attention to an event in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the top, I think. And --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm -- yes. Here we are. It's at the bottom there. It's at the bottom of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: "A number of incidents occurred in the border region stretching from Djakovica to Prizren. Near midnight on the 27th of January, a six-man police patrol encountered and exchanged fire with an armed group of men in the Djakovica area." So this is the area north of Prizren in the west of the country, close to the Albanian border. Two policemen were injured and two members of the other group, allegedly KLA, were killed. I believe that this event is linked to the events that took place at Rogovo 24 hours later, because this is all in the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Rogovo is a significant incident even if it has to some degree been shadowed by events?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We may look at the detail of that and look at some photographs of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's now 4.00. I wonder if the interpreters agree we might sit until ten past.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ten past.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 216.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: If I can go back to earlier in the day when we had again been trying to meet with the Regional Centre heads. It seemed every time I met with them, we had another tram smash, but we were told that again something bad had just happened in -- in Rogovo. This was only a few minutes' drive from where we were in Prizren, and so I went straight there as soon as we realised that the initial reports were getting worse and it was moving up to the scale of deaths and becoming a major incident. When I got to the village at about twenty past one, Loncar was there already and was clearly in charge. He was giving orders to the policemen who were there, and they were going to him with questions which he answered in a way that indicated that he was in command. The policemen were broadly of two sorts. They were what I would call normal policemen in their blue uniforms, and there was a group who were wearing light grey coveralls, like a grey-blue, like a jumpsuit. I believe they had a shoulder patch. And it was my firm impression that they were a specialist anti-terrorist unit because we had never seen people in this uniform carrying out normal police duties. They were also fitter, better armed, and more cohesive, better trained than the normal police. And while we were there, they were leaving the location. We were held outside the compound, which was a walled farmyard with a large gate, and we were held outside that until an investigating judge had been brought from Djakovica and he carried out his inspection. And his inspection, I have to say, was extremely short and cursory in view of what was inside and needed to be inspected. But in the -- when we were allowed into the courtyard of the farmyard, we came across a minibus which had got at that stage five bodies inside it with two other ones just outside the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it will be easier, if potentially a little distressing for some, to look at tab 71. You may be able to give your narrative by reference to these photographs.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are six of them in all. Seven -- six. You simply choose the one that enables you to tell the story first. It's probably the one ending in the figure 59, being the bus itself. That will be a view of the bus.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That is the sight that I saw when I went into the -- into the compound. And as you can see, there are a number of dead people inside Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the bus. And there is a quite considerable pool of blood down here, which is being added to by the contents of the bus, coming out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: There were five bodies in the bus at the time and two close to it, five other bodies in a shed nearby. And as we were there, the bodies were being assembled rather like the catch at the end of a day's grouse shooting, perhaps. And you can see here also this policeman whose uniform is expressly not the normal police uniform. This is the light grey coveralls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you described the uniform of people who were leaving on your arrival.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The specialist, fitter-looking men.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That is this sort of uniform --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This the sort of uniform.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: -- they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you able to give us any -- it's almost visible what the marking on the armband was.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly red, white, and blue, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The positioning the firearms beside the bodies, did you see anything that explained all that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The firearms were placed next to the bodies, but these bodies by this stage had all been moved. There were -- I counted 12 weapons, whereas there were, I think, 25 dead. General Loncar stated to me they were all armed, but I made a point of counting the weapons and only got to 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Footwear, was that of any significance at this site, in your judgement, or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, here you can see that this -- this man here is wearing his wellington boots, which again are not the best footwear for going over the hills. Here you can see someone wearing his indoor slippers. This man is wearing his indoor slippers. So whatever else they were doing at the time, they were not -- they were not dressed for fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Anything else in the -- there's another general photograph, the one with the tractor in the background that shows the scene, and it also shows some more uniforms. No, not that one. The one with the tractor in the background.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Sorry. That's this one. That's the top of this one, I think, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's that one as well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Here you can see the different uniforms. That's a VJ soldier, and then here are -- there's our man in the -- in the grey jumpsuit. That is normal police combat uniform, and here is the local traffic cop. So that, I think, gives an indication of the degree to which the uniforms were different. And the ones we were normally seeing were perhaps that one and that one, and this one was only seen on this one occasion and one earlier sighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the man in the centre of the picture in the green?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Is a Yugoslav army soldier, and I think was probably accompanying Loncar. I think he was part of his party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at Exhibit -- tab 41.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is the report from Prizren to the OSCE headquarters in Pristina, and this describes the events at Rogovo where, as I've stated, 25 Albanians were killed and one policeman was killed, one Serbian policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that this contemporaneous reporting comments on the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. If I can take you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Some conclusions that can be drawn already: "The amount of force employed was not proportional. Not all persons were KLA. There is little evidence of fighting back, as there is also little evidence of a large number of weapons. There are also many questions. Why was the MUP in this village at 6.00 in the morning? Where would the KLA come from?" and so on. I think the point that is worth reflecting on is that, firstly, with 25 people killed on the Kosovo Albanian side, this is not what normally happens in an exchange of fire. In a normal exchange of fire between two sides, you can expect to have at least as many wounded as are killed, if not more wounded than are killed. And so it was unusual that nobody appeared to have only been wounded in this, and we were suspicious that not everybody had been killed fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No one captured alive?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No one was captured alive. And again, the bullet holes, the number of bullet holes in the minibus and the damage that it had actually sustained do not suggest any attempt to take prisoners or to use restraint by the security forces. The other fact is that the forensic examination by the investigating judge took about an hour and five minutes at the most, and you've seen in the photos that the place was pretty well ankle deep in mud, slush, and blood, and therefore an attempt to do a proper forensic examination of this site should properly have taken a long time and appears never to have been done. So I think it is my conclusion that these people that were killed may have been associated with the KLA, or some of them may have been, but they appear not to have fought back very significantly, otherwise more people would have been injured on the -- on the police side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have covered a lot of territory today, and of course by dealing with the history of the OSCE through this witness, we will be able to take later witnesses who cover the similar territory much more swiftly. I am happy to say that he, although inconvenient, I know, will be able to be here on Monday, because I believe tomorrow we're only sitting until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're sitting tomorrow between 9.00 and just after 1.00. So it's not a full day. How long do you anticipate you'll be in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would hope to conclude his evidence by the first or, it may be, the only break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. At 9.00 tomorrow morning, please, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 12th day of April, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.13 p.m.,
